query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Accelerated coupled degradation in multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloys under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures is primarily driven by wear-induced disruption of a protective oxide (passivation) layer. Once disrupted, the fresh metal surface is rapidly corroded by the aggressive environment, further weakening the layer and thereby accelerating both wear and corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with a naturally formed, albeit fragile, oxide layer acquired during fabrication at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Application of a pre-treatment designed to stabilize and reinforce the oxide/passivation layer prior to wear-corrosion testing, compared with untreated baseline samples.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature in a corrosive electrolyte environment with controlled wear cycles; sufficient oxygen availability to enable in situ formation and disruption of oxide layers.
generation.structural_mediator: The continuity and stability of the surface oxide/passivation layer.
generation.mechanism: During wear, the protective oxide layer is intermittently removed, exposing fresh metal. This exposure accelerates localized corrosion which further undermines the oxide regeneration, thereby synergistically enhancing overall degradation through the mutual reinforcement of mechanical damage and chemical attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Pre-treated samples with enhanced oxide stability will exhibit lower total degradation, reduced wear rates, and diminished corrosion rates relative to the baseline samples that possess a less stable oxide layer.
generation.baseline: Multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy samples with the native oxide layer and no additional passivation pre-treatment.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under conditions of elevated temperature, exposure to corrosive electrolyte (e.g., NaCl solution), and under wear conditions that are sufficient to disrupt the native oxide but not so severe as to cause complete mechanical removal of the substrate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the differences in wear and corrosion rates between treated and untreated samples is uncertain due to possible variability in microstructural heterogeneity and the kinetics of oxide film reformation under dynamic conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of coupled wear-corrosion experiments at elevated temperatures using in situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and wear-track imaging on two sets of alloy samples: one set receiving a passivation pre-treatment to enhance oxide stability and a control set without the treatment. Ensure identical testing conditions for both sets with respect to temperature, corrosive environment, and wear cycle parameters.
measurements: Total degradation quantified by weight loss or volumetric measurements
Wear rate determined from wear track dimensions and imaging
Corrosion rate measured via corrosion current density and polarization resistance
Continuity and integrity of the oxide layer monitored in situ using EIS and high-resolution imaging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no statistically significant reduction in total degradation, wear rate, and corrosion rate in the pre-treated samples compared to the untreated control under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis that wear-induced oxide disruption is the primary mechanism for accelerated degradation will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

Thus, if cooperative heterostructures capable of releasing frictional stress in stages are configured in the alloy, it is expected to suppress the sliding-induced deformation. In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. chosen.technique: coupled wear-corrosion experiment utilizing in situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and wear-track imaging to monitor real-time oxide layer removal
chosen.conditions: elevated temperature in a corrosive electrolyte concurrently subjected to controlled wear cycles, with one set of alloy samples receiving a pre-treatment to enhance oxide integrity and a matched baseline with no such treatment
chosen.why: This approach directly tests the mechanistic hypothesis that accelerated coupled degradation stems from wear-induced disruption of a protective oxide layer, which then intensifies corrosion. By controlling the oxide layer’s stability via pre-treatment and comparing the degradation profiles (total degradation, wear rate, and corrosion rate) against a baseline, the experiment provides a clear falsification criterion if no significant differences in performance are observed.
